title: Passive and reflexive
intro: Turkish changes the **voice** of a verb with a suffix placed right after the stem, before any tense or ending. This unit adds two such suffixes: the passive (*yapıldı*, it was built), which also makes the impersonal passive for rules and general statements (*Burada sigara içilmez*, No smoking here), and the reflexive (*giyindi*, she got dressed). It ends with *kendi*, **self**, for everything the reflexive suffix can't say.

blocks.text: A passive verb tells what happened to someone or something, usually without saying who did it: *Cami 1557'de tamamlandı* (The mosque was completed in 1557). The passive suffix comes right after the stem, and every tense, ending and form of the earlier units can follow it: *yapılıyor, yapıldı, yapılacak, yapılmış*.

blocks.text: **Stem changes.** *Gitmek* and *etmek* soften before the vowel, as they do before any vowel: *gidilmek*, *edilmek*. So every verb made with *etmek* has its passive in *edilmek*: *davet edildim* (I was invited), *inşa edildi* (it was built). *Yemek* and *demek* take *-n*: *yenmek*, *denmek*; *söylemek* gives *söylenmek*.

blocks.text: A passive stem always has more than one syllable, so its aorist is `-Ir`: *yapılır*, *okunur*, *bulunur*, never *yapılar*.
**The object becomes the subject**, so it loses its accusative: *Mektubu yazdım* (I wrote the letter) → *Mektup yazıldı* (The letter was written).

**Who did it.** Most passive sentences leave the doer out. To name it, put *tarafından* (by) after the noun: *Süleymaniye Mimar Sinan tarafından yapıldı* (The Süleymaniye was built by Mimar Sinan). It sounds formal, at home in history books, the news and official letters; in conversation Turkish prefers the active: *Süleymaniye'yi Mimar Sinan yaptı*. With a pronoun it takes the genitive: *benim tarafımdan*, *onun tarafından*.

**Participles and -mIş adjectives** are built on passive verbs too: *1557'de tamamlanan cami* (the mosque completed in 1557), *kırılmış bardak* (a broken glass), *haşlanmış yumurta* (a boiled egg), the words [B1 unit 3](gp-mis-adjective) promised.

items.en: The mosque was completed in 1557.
My wallet has been found!
This bridge was built in the 16th century.
We were invited to the wedding.
The meeting has been postponed until tomorrow.
This book is widely read.

blocks.text: After a stem in l the suffix is `-In`, not `-Il`: *bulundu*, *alındı*, *bilinir*. *Bululdu* doesn't exist.

blocks.title: Bulunmak
blocks.text: *Bulunmak* has a life of its own. Besides **to be found**, it means **to be (somewhere)** in careful Turkish: *Müze şehir merkezinde bulunuyor* (The museum is in the city centre). Many other passives also serve as plain intransitive verbs: *Kapı açıldı* (The door opened), *Ders bitti, okul kapandı*.

sections.title: Burada sigara içilmez: rules and general statements

blocks.text: Turkish also makes a passive from verbs without an object, which English can't do: *gidilir* (literally **it is gone**), *oturulur*, *girilmez*. The result has no subject at all and speaks of people in general: *Oraya otobüsle gidilir* (You get there by bus). This is the impersonal passive.

**In the aorist** it states a rule, a custom or the right way to do something: *Burada yüzülmez* (No swimming here), *Camiye ayakkabıyla girilmez* (You don't go into a mosque with your shoes on). An ordinary passive with a general subject does the same job: *Burada sigara içilmez* (No smoking here), *Türkiye'de misafire çay ikram edilir* (In Turkey, guests are offered tea).

**Questions** ask how things are done: *Oraya nasıl gidilir?* (How do you get there?), *Bu kelime nasıl yazılır?* (How is this word spelled?), *Bu nasıl okunur?* (How do you pronounce this?), *Buna Türkçede ne denir?* (What's this called in Turkish?).

**Recipes and instructions** give their steps in the passive aorist: *Önce soğanlar doğranır ve yağa eklenir* (First the onions are chopped and added to the oil). *Su kaynayınca yumurtalar eklenir* (When the water boils, the eggs go in).
The doer is everyone, so *tarafından* never appears, and the verb stays in the third person singular.

items.en: How do you get there?
No swimming here.
How is this word spelled?
What do you call this in Turkish?
At bayram, people kiss the hands of their elders.
First the onions are chopped.

blocks.title: Denir and yenir
blocks.text: *Demek* and *yemek* give *denir* (it is said, it's called; also *denilir*) and *yenir* (it is eaten, it's edible): *Bu mantar yenir mi?* (Is this mushroom edible?).
An impersonal passive has no person: *Oraya otobüsle gidilir*, never *gidiliriz*. To include yourself, use the active: *Oraya otobüsle gideriz* (We go there by bus).

A small group of verbs take `-(I)n` for an action you do to yourself (*dönüşlü çatı*): *yıkamak* (to wash) → *yıkanmak* (to have a wash), *giymek* (to put on) → *giyinmek* (to get dressed), *hazırlamak* (to prepare) → *hazırlanmak* (to get ready). After a vowel the suffix is just *-n*.

blocks.text: **Passive or reflexive?** After a vowel, and after l, the two suffixes look the same, so some forms have two readings: *yıkandı* can be **he had a wash** or **it was washed**. The subject decides: *Çocuk yıkandı* (The child had a wash, or was given one), but *Araba yıkandı* (The car was washed).

**No object.** A reflexive verb already contains its object. For one piece of clothing, use the plain verb: *Ceketimi giydim* (I put on my jacket), but *Giyindim* (I got dressed). The same goes for parts of the body: *Ellerimi yıkadım* (I washed my hands).

items.en: I'm getting dressed right now; wait five minutes.
We're getting ready for the wedding.
She combed her hair in front of the mirror.
Have the children had their bath?
I had a shower and got dressed.

blocks.text: French marks these verbs with se: se laver, s'habiller, se préparer; Turkish has one suffix for the same idea: *yıkanmak, giyinmek, hazırlanmak*. But many French reflexives are plain verbs in Turkish: se lever is *kalkmak*, se promener is *gezmek*.
A few verbs with this suffix have meanings of their own today: *görünmek* (to seem, to look: *Yorgun görünüyorsun*, You look tired) and *bulunmak* (to be located).

For **myself, yourself** and the rest, Turkish uses *kendi* with a possessive ending, then whatever case the verb needs: *Aynada kendime baktım* (I looked at myself in the mirror), *Kendini nasıl hissediyorsun?* (How do you feel?). Most actions have no reflexive verb, so *kendi* is the usual way to say **-self**.

In the third person singular, the short forms *kendini, kendine, kendinden* are more common in speech than *kendisini, kendisine, kendisinden*, so *kendini* can mean **yourself** or **himself, herself**; context decides.

**Kendi + noun: own.** Before a noun, bare *kendi* means **own**, and the noun keeps its possessive ending: *kendi evim* (my own house), *kendi arabası* (her own car), *Kendi odan var mı?* (Do you have your own room?).

**Myself, in person.** Alone as a subject, *kendim, kendin, kendisi* stress who did it: *Bu pastayı kendim yaptım* (I made this cake myself), *Müdürün kendisi geldi* (The director came in person). *Kendisi* is also a polite way to refer to someone: *Kendisi şu anda toplantıda* (He's in a meeting at the moment).

**Set phrases.** *Kendi kendine* means **by itself, on one's own** or **to oneself**: *Kapı kendi kendine açıldı* (The door opened by itself), *Kendi kendine konuşuyor* (He's talking to himself). *Kendi başına* means **on one's own, alone**: *Kendi başına mı geldin?* (Did you come on your own?). And *Kendine iyi bak* (Take care of yourself) is an everyday goodbye.

items.en: I looked at myself in the mirror.
I feel very tired today.
I made this cake myself.
Do you have your own room?
The door opened by itself.
Take care of yourself!

blocks.text: Use either the reflexive verb or *kendi*, not both: *Yıkandım* (I had a wash), not *Kendimi yıkandım*. And *kendi* before a noun needs the possessive on the noun: *kendi evim*, not *kendi ev*.

summary: The passive comes right after the stem: `-Il` after consonants (*yapıldı*), `-In` after l (*bulundu*), *-n* after vowels (*okundu*); *gid-il-*, *ed-il-*.
The object of the active becomes the subject, without its accusative: *Mektup yazıldı*; *tarafından* names the doer, formally: *Sinan tarafından yapıldı*.
Verbs without an object have an impersonal passive for people in general: *Oraya nasıl gidilir?*, *Burada yüzülmez*, *Buna ne denir?*
Rules, customs and recipes use the passive aorist, `-Ir` in the positive: *Soğanlar doğranır*, *Sigara içilmez*.
A few verbs take `-(I)n` as a reflexive and take no object: *yıkanmak, giyinmek, soyunmak, hazırlanmak, taranmak*.
*Kendi* + possessive is **myself, yourself…**, with any case: *kendimi, kendine*; *kendi* + possessed noun is **own**: *kendi evim*.
*Kendi kendine* (by itself, to oneself), *kendi başına* (on one's own), *Kendine iyi bak!* (Take care!).
